summary.text: At the seventh step, exact division would require \(171\mid 2^N+1\), where \(N=332572817028187686275682948600327513806149983112761\) is the sixth term. But \(19\mid171\), while \(N\equiv3\pmod{18}\) and \(2^{18}\equiv1\pmod{19}\), so \(2^N+1\equiv2^3+1=9\not\equiv0\pmod{19}\).

full_proof.text:
Let the sequence be defined by
\[
a(1)=a(2)=1,\qquad a(n)=\frac{2^{a(n-1)}+1}{a(n-2)}.
\]
For this recurrence to continue to produce integers, at every index \(n\geq 3\) the positive integer \(a(n-2)\) must divide \(2^{a(n-1)}+1\). We show that this divisibility fails when one tries to form \(a(7)\).

First compute the initial terms. They are
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(3)&=\frac{2^{a(2)}+1}{a(1)}=\frac{2^1+1}{1}=3,\\
a(4)&=\frac{2^{a(3)}+1}{a(2)}=\frac{2^3+1}{1}=9,\\
a(5)&=\frac{2^{a(4)}+1}{a(3)}=\frac{2^9+1}{3}
      =\frac{513}{3}=171.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the next term is
\[
a(6)=\frac{2^{171}+1}{9}.
\]
This quotient is an integer. We will establish this, and at the same time determine its residue modulo \(18\), by working modulo \(162=9\cdot18\).

We begin modulo \(81\). Direct calculation gives
\[
2^9=512\equiv 26\pmod{81}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
2^{18}\equiv 26^2=676\equiv 28\pmod{81},
\]
because \(676=8\cdot81+28\). Multiplying the residues for \(2^{18}\) and \(2^9\), we obtain
\[
2^{27}\equiv 28\cdot26=728\equiv -1\pmod{81},
\]
since \(728=9\cdot81-1\). Squaring gives
\[
2^{54}\equiv 1\pmod{81}.
\]
As \(171=3\cdot54+9\), it follows that
\[
2^{171}=\bigl(2^{54}\bigr)^3 2^9\equiv 2^9\equiv26\pmod{81}.
\]
Both \(2^{171}\) and \(26\) are even. Their difference is therefore divisible by \(2\), as well as by \(81\). Since \(2\) and \(81\) are coprime, their difference is divisible by \(162\). Hence the preceding congruence strengthens to
\[
2^{171}\equiv26\pmod{162}.
\]
Adding one yields
\[
2^{171}+1\equiv27\pmod{162}.
\]
In particular, \(9\mid 2^{171}+1\), so \(a(6)\) is indeed an integer. Put
\[
A=a(6)=\frac{2^{171}+1}{9}.
\]
The congruence just obtained says
\[
9A\equiv27=9\cdot3\pmod{162}.
\]
Equivalently, \(162\mid9(A-3)\). Cancelling the common factor \(9\) gives
\[
18\mid A-3,
\]
and therefore
\[
A\equiv3\pmod{18}.
\]

For completeness, the exact integer is
\[
A=332572817028187686275682948600327513806149983112761.
\]
Indeed,
\[
2^{171}=2993155353253689176481146537402947624255349848014848,
\]
and multiplication gives
\[
9A=2993155353253689176481146537402947624255349848014849
   =2^{171}+1.
\]
The modular argument above is what will matter for the next recurrence step.

Now consider the numerator that would be used to form \(a(7)\):
\[
2^{a(6)}+1=2^A+1.
\]
Because \(a(5)=171=9\cdot19\), exactness of the seventh recurrence step would require
\[
171\mid 2^A+1.
\]
In particular, it would require \(19\mid2^A+1\).

However, Fermat's little theorem gives
\[
2^{18}\equiv1\pmod{19},
\]
since \(19\) is prime and does not divide \(2\). We have already proved that \(A\equiv3\pmod{18}\), so write \(A=18q+3\) for some nonnegative integer \(q\). Then
\[
2^A=2^{18q+3}=(2^{18})^q2^3\equiv1^q\cdot8=8\pmod{19}.
\]
It follows that
\[
2^A+1\equiv8+1=9\pmod{19}.
\]
Since \(9\not\equiv0\pmod{19}\), the integer \(19\) does not divide \(2^A+1\). Therefore \(171\), which is itself divisible by \(19\), cannot divide \(2^A+1\).

Thus
\[
a(7)=\frac{2^{a(6)}+1}{a(5)}=\frac{2^A+1}{171}
\]
is not an integer. The recurrence therefore fails to have integer values at its seventh term, disproving the conjecture that every term \(a(n)\) is an integer.
